Subject: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification — hosted API vs current provider

Hi Alex / Samira — thanks again for the time today. Quick post-call recap and proposed next steps so we all have the same view.

Recap (from our discussion)
- FinLytics target: end-to-end p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 500ms for typical text-gen requests (prompt size ~120 tokens, response size 30–60 tokens).
- Streaming: you rely on client-side streaming; critical metric is first-byte latency (time-to-first-token) and steady-state per-token latency for long responses.
- Current provider baseline (what you shared): p95 ~320ms, p99 ~780ms (see attached current-provider-p95-report.csv).
- Concurrency/throughput: production peak is ~120 concurrent sessions, average sustained concurrency ~40, bursts up to 200 for trading hours.

Questions / clarifications we promised to confirm
1) Definition of end-to-end you want us to measure (client->first-token, client->last-token, or server-only).
2) Where synthetic tests should originate from (we can run from us-west-2 and us-east-1 — confirm which region matters).
3) Streaming semantics: do you need sub-200ms first-byte at p95, or is p95 for whole response acceptable?

Proposed next steps
- You to share the load profile and any blackbox tests you’ve run (I see Samira asked for that during the call).
- We (Marissa/Aditya) will put together a 15–30 minute benchmark plan and run a hosted vs. your current-provider side-by-side for the same prompt set and concurrency pattern.
- Schedule a 45-minute technical deep-dive to review results and define any routing/fallback policies — propose May 17th 10:00am PT, let me know if that works.

Attachments: current-provider-p95-report.csv (you provided), we’ll attach a Redwood test plan next.

Thanks —

Thanks Laura — appreciate the recap. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 

- End-to-end: when we say p95/p99 we mean client-observed end-to-end (client submits request -> client receives first token for streaming; and client receives final token for full-response checks). In other words, please include edge hops and any gateway latency we would see in production.
- Regions: us-west-2 is primary, us-east-1 is secondary — please run primary tests from us-west-2.
- Streaming: our main requirement is a fast time-to-first-byte (TTFB). For short assistant responses (<=60 tokens) we want p95 first-byte < 250ms. For long-running streaming (100+ tokens) we care about steady-state per-token latency and jitter (we see spikes today).

I’ve attached the load profile JSON and a sampling of production traces (see finlytics-load-profile.json). We’re happy to run in parallel with your hosted tests.

Alex

Hi Alex / Samira — thanks for sending the load profile and traces. I’m Marissa (Performance Lead) — wanted to add technical detail so we’re aligned on measurement definitions and the planned bench approach. Attaching our redwood-latency-test-plan.pdf with specifics.

Measurement definitions (what Redwood will report)
- First-byte (TTFB) p95/p99: time from HTTP POST completion on the client side to the arrival of the first model token payload (includes edge/gateway + runtime).
- Full-response (end-to-end) p95/p99: time from client POST to receipt of final token (includes streaming time if applicable).
- Per-token steady-state: median and p95 of inter-token arrival times for streaming responses longer than 80 tokens.
- Server-only vs client-observed: by default we’ll run client-observed tests (we instrument the client to include RTT to our edge). We can also share server-only internal metrics if you want to decompose.

Planned benchmark parameters
- Region: us-west-2 (as requested).
- Prompt set: your supplied prompts (we’ll mirror token distribution).
- Concurrency scenarios: 1) sustained 40 concurrent sessions (your avg), 2) burst 120 concurrent sessions, 3) stress 200 concurrent sessions for 10 minutes.
- Model variants: we’ll test the hosted Redwood catalog model most similar to your current provider model (we’ll list exact model IDs in the plan).
- Warm cache vs cold runs: we’ll run both — cold start emphasis for p99 spikes, warm-cache for steady-state.

What to expect / caveats
- Network variability: client side network noise can inflate p99; we mitigate by running multiple repeated windows and reporting median p95/p99 across windows.
- Streaming differences: some providers buffer tokens server-side to improve throughput; that reduces per-token jitter but increases TTFB. We’ll present first-byte + per-token metrics so you can choose the right tradeoff.

Requested items from FinLytics
- Confirm the two canonical test prompts you want used for the short (<=60 token) and long (100+ token) cases.
- Confirm that us-west-2 originates are acceptable.

Next steps
- We’ll run the side-by-side benchmark (hosted Redwood vs. your current provider) and post results before the deep-dive.
- Deliverable: a 1-page comparison (p95/p99 first-byte + full-response) + raw CSVs.

Thanks — I’ll attach the test plan now and start scheduling the runs once we’ve got the prompts.

—Marissa
